chapters.title: The Page That Hid
chapters.focus: irony and tone · idiom · implied meaning · sophisticated cohesion

pages.text: The Starlight Library had a reputation for swallowing visitors whole — not literally, the guidebooks hastened to add, but scholars who wandered in for an afternoon had been known to [[resurface|appear again after being gone a long time]] decades later, blinking and bearded. It was here, among a million muttering volumes, that the final page was said to lie.

q.q: What is the tone of the opening paragraph?
options: humorous exaggeration
genuine fear
dry scientific description
bitter criticism
q.explain: Scholars resurfacing “decades later, blinking and bearded” is comic exaggeration, and “not literally” winks at the reader.

pages.text: Its guardian, an ancient dragon called Vellum, was courteous to the point of [[absurdity|being silly or ridiculous]]. “By all means search,” he purred, “though I should warn you that the page has hidden itself. Pages do that, when they have been through a great deal. It will come out only for someone who has understood what the other five were trying to say.”

q.q: According to Vellum, what will make the page come out?
options: someone seeing what links the other pages
a careful search of every single shelf
the dragon's formal permission to take it
reading the five pages aloud in order
q.explain: “Only for someone who has understood what the other five were trying to say.”

pages.text: {hero} sat down and laid the five pages side by side. A sleepy meadow; a greedy little dragon forgiven; a riddle in a hollow tree; a serpent freed from somebody else's carelessness; a council talked round. It dawned on {hero} that not one page had been won by force. Each had been [[earned|got because you deserved it through your actions]] through kindness, patience or wit.

options: No page was won by force.
The pages follow a fixed order.
Each realm tried to keep its page.
Dragons appear in most chapters.
q.explain: “Not one page had been won by force. Each had been earned through kindness, patience or wit.”

pages.text: “Kindness, patience and wit,” {hero} said aloud. There was a rustle high above, and a page fluttered down like a falling leaf, settling in {hero}'s hands. Vellum inclined his great head. “Few manage it,” he said. “Most come looking for the page; you came looking for the point.” The Storybook closed with a contented sigh, whole at last — and {pet}, who had slept through the entire [[ordeal|a very difficult, unpleasant experience]], chose that moment to wake up.

q.q: What does Vellum mean by “you came looking for the point”?
options: {hero} sought the meaning, not the object.
{hero} wanted the sharpest page.
{hero} came to argue with him.
{hero} brought a map of the library.
q.explain: A play on words: others hunt the page itself; {hero} looked for its meaning (“the point”).

final.q: Why is {pet}'s waking up at the very end funny?
options: It sleeps through it all, then wakes when it's over.
It wakes just in time to find the page.
It finally frightens the dragon away.
It wakes up and reads the book aloud.
final.explain: Comic timing: {pet} misses the whole adventure and wakes the moment everything is solved.

chapters.title: The Book That Wouldn't End
chapters.focus: irony and understatement · idiom · implied meaning

pages.text: Vellum, it emerged, had a confession to make. Somewhere in the Starlight Library was a novel that refused to finish. Every time a reader reached its last page, a fresh chapter would [[sprout|appear and start growing suddenly]] from the spine, and the story would trundle on. “Delightful for the first three hundred years,” the dragon sighed, “somewhat less so since.”

q.q: What is Vellum's attitude to the endless book?
options: weary, expressed with dry humour
thrilled by its endless chapters
frightened of what it might do
indifferent, as if it hardly matters
q.explain: “Delightful for the first three hundred years… somewhat less so since” is understatement: he's tired of it, and says so wryly.

notes.thrilled by its endless chapters: “Somewhat less so since” tells us the delight wore off long ago.
notes.frightened of what it might do: He sighs; he isn't afraid. It's tiredness, not fear.
notes.indifferent, as if it hardly matters: He raised the problem himself, so it clearly matters to him.

pages.text: {hero} opened the book at random. It was, by any standard, a muddle: a princess who had been rescued eleven times, a villain who had retired, returned and retired again, and a talking teapot who appeared to have [[lost the thread|stopped following what was happening]] entirely. The characters seemed exhausted. One of them had written in the margin, in tiny letters: “Please let us stop.”

q.q: The note in the margin suggests that…
options: the characters themselves want the story to end
a previous reader scribbled a complaint
the teapot had written the whole book
the villain was hoping to come back for a third time
q.explain: It was written by “one of them”: the tired characters are asking for an ending.

notes.a previous reader scribbled a complaint: The text says “one of them”, meaning one of the exhausted characters.
notes.the teapot had written the whole book: The teapot had “lost the thread”. It isn't the author.
notes.the villain was hoping to come back for: The villain had already come back once. The note asks to stop, not to carry on.

pages.text: It struck {hero} that no one had ever asked the characters what ending they would like. Every reader had simply turned the page and hoped. So, with Vellum's [[blessing|permission and good wishes]], {hero} read the last page aloud and then asked, quite politely, what they wanted. The answer came at once, in a chorus of small voices: “A picnic. With everyone. And then nothing else at all.”

q.q: What did {hero} do that no reader had done before?
options: asked the characters how it should end
read the entire book cover to cover in one evening
wrote a brand-new final chapter
hid the book from the dragon
q.explain: “No one had ever asked the characters what ending they would like.”

notes.read the entire book cover to cover in o: {hero} only opened it “at random” and read the last page aloud.
notes.wrote a brand-new final chapter: {hero} didn't invent the ending. The characters chose it.
notes.hid the book from the dragon: {hero} acted “with Vellum's blessing”, not behind his back.

pages.text: {hero} wrote the picnic onto the last page in careful handwriting: the princess, the twice-retired villain and the teapot, sharing sandwiches on a hill. For a moment the book hesitated. Then it closed with a soft, [[contented|happy and satisfied]] thump, and no new chapter grew. “Three hundred years of plot,” Vellum murmured, “and all it wanted was lunch.” {pet}, curled on a cushion, slept through this chapter too.

q.q: Why is Vellum's final remark ironic?
options: A grand, endless story wanted something very ordinary.
Vellum had planned the picnic ending all along.
The characters were hungry because nobody had ever fed them.
The book had always been a cookbook in disguise.
q.explain: Three hundred years of plot, and the wish was just “lunch”: a huge story with a tiny, ordinary wish.

notes.Vellum had planned the picnic ending all: Vellum had no answer himself. It was {hero} who asked the characters.
notes.The characters were hungry because nobod: The joke isn't hunger. It's the gap between a huge story and a tiny wish.
notes.The book had always been a cookbook in d: It's a novel with a princess and a villain, not a cookbook.

final.q: If you have “lost the thread”, you have…
options: stopped following what is going on
dropped your sewing needle
run out of things to say
fallen out with a good friend
final.explain: Lost the thread = lost track of what is happening, like the muddled teapot.

notes.dropped your sewing needle: It's an idiom: there's no real thread or needle.
notes.run out of things to say: Close, but this idiom is about losing track of the story, not having nothing to say.
notes.fallen out with a good friend: That's a different idiom, about an argument.
